findings.title: The queue shutdown API is unavailable on supported Python versions
findings.body: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, an exception raised by `result_processor` causes evaluation of `queue.ShutDown` in this handler to raise `AttributeError`, terminating the worker thread; and shutdown cannot wake workers blocked in `Queue.get()` because `q.shutdown()` raises `AttributeError` and is only logged. This makes the new mode leave daemon workers behind on shutdown and permanently stop processing a queue after its first processing exception. Use a version-compatible sentinel/wakeup mechanism (or require and enforce Python 3.13) instead.

findings.title: Failed result processing is acknowledged and committed
findings.body: The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` but unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit thread will then advance the Kafka offset past the failed message, so transient database/API failures lose the result instead of allowing it to be retried. This also contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Only complete an offset after a successful processor return, or explicitly route failures through the consumer's retry/DLQ policy.

findings.title: Worker queues are unbounded, so slow processing has no backpressure
findings.body: Each queue is created with `queue.Queue()` without a `maxsize`. Consequently the Kafka consumer can continue accepting records while a slow queue is backlogged, accumulating an unbounded number of decoded messages and retained payloads in memory. Under the slow-item condition this feature is intended to handle, this can exhaust process memory rather than applying the documented natural backpressure. Configure a bounded queue size and integrate full-queue behavior with upstream polling/backpressure.

findings.title: Invalid negative max-workers silently drops every queued message
findings.body: The CLI accepts arbitrary integers for `--max-workers`, and a negative value is truthy here, so `FixedQueuePool` is created with zero queues. Every subsequent submit then raises a modulo-by-zero error in `get_queue_for_group`; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that error and marks the Kafka offset complete, causing all messages to be committed without processing. Validate `max_workers > 0` before constructing the pool (and do not silently substitute 20 for an explicitly supplied zero value).
